title: Amplifier Basics
description: Model a real amplifier by its input resistance, output resistance and open-circuit gain, and compute gains, loading, cascades and efficiency.

study.title: Voltage gain
study.body: An amplifier takes an input signal $v_i(t)$ and delivers $v_o(t) = A_v v_i(t)$ with the same waveshape. If $A_v > 0$ it is **noninverting**; if $A_v < 0$ it is **inverting** (the output is the input flipped upside down). One input terminal and one output terminal are usually tied to a common ground.

study.title: Voltage-amplifier model
study.body: A real amplifier is modelled by three parameters: the **input resistance** $R_i$ (seen looking into the input), a voltage-controlled source $A_{voc}v_i$, and the **output resistance** $R_o$ in series with the output. $A_{voc}$ is the **open-circuit voltage gain**: the gain when no load is connected (no current in $R_o$).

study.title: Loading effects
study.body: Two voltage dividers reduce the gain you actually get. At the input, $R_s$ and $R_i$ divide $v_s$; at the output, $R_o$ and $R_L$ divide $A_{voc}v_i$. So the loaded gain $A_v = v_o/v_i$ and the overall gain $A_{vs} = v_o/v_s$ are smaller than $A_{voc}$. An **ideal voltage amplifier** has $R_i \to \infty$ and $R_o \to 0$, so there is no loading at all.

study.title: Current gain, power gain and decibels
study.body: With $i_i = v_i/R_i$ and $i_o = v_o/R_L$ the current gain is $A_i = A_v R_i/R_L$, and the power gain is $G = P_o/P_i = A_v A_i$. Gains are often given in decibels: $|A_v|_{dB} = 20\log_{10}|A_v|$ for voltage (or current) ratios, $G_{dB} = 10\log_{10}G$ for power ratios. Example: $A_v = 100$ is 40 dB; $G = 10^6$ is 60 dB.

study.title: Cascaded amplifiers
study.body: When stage 1 drives stage 2, the overall gain is the product of the stage gains, $A_v = A_{v1}A_{v2}$ (so dB values add). Each stage gain must include loading: the input resistance $R_{i2}$ of stage 2 is the load of stage 1. The simplified model of the cascade has $R_i = R_{i1}$, $R_o = R_{o,last}$ and $A_{voc}$ computed with the last stage open-circuited.

study.title: Power supplies and efficiency
study.body: The extra output power comes from the dc supplies: $P_s = V_{AA}I_A + V_{BB}I_B$. Power balance: $P_i + P_s = P_o + P_d$, where $P_d$ is dissipated as heat. The input power $P_i$ is usually negligible. Efficiency is the fraction of supply power that reaches the load.

steps.title: What an amplifier does
steps.body:
An amplifier makes a signal bigger without changing its shape: $v_o(t) = A_v v_i(t)$.
- $A_v > 0$: **noninverting**, output in phase with the input.
- $A_v < 0$: **inverting**, output is the input flipped upside down.

steps.prompt: An amplifier has voltage gain $A_v$ = {{A}}. The input is $v_i(t) = {{Vm}}\sin(\omega t)$ V. What is the output?
steps.explanation: Multiply the input by the gain: $v_o = A_v v_i$ = ({{A}}) × {{Vm}} $\sin(\omega t)$ = {{A*Vm}} $\sin(\omega t)$ V. The minus sign means this is an inverting amplifier: the output is an upside-down, larger copy of the input.

steps.title: The voltage-amplifier model
steps.body:
A real amplifier draws some current from the source and its output voltage sags under load. We model it with:
- $R_i$: the **input resistance** across the input terminals
- $A_{voc}v_i$: a voltage-controlled voltage source
- $R_o$: the **output resistance** in series with the output
With the output open ($R_L = \infty$) no current flows in $R_o$, so $v_o = A_{voc}v_i$: $A_{voc}$ is the **open-circuit voltage gain**.

steps.prompt: A voltage amplifier is connected between a signal source and a load. Tap the resistors that belong to the **amplifier model** itself.
steps.explanation:
The amplifier model has three parts: the **input resistance** across its input terminals ($R_2$, the voltage across it is $v_i$), a controlled source $A_{voc}v_i$, and the **output resistance** in series with that source ($R_3$).
$R_1$ is the internal resistance of the signal source and $R_4$ is the load; they are outside the amplifier.

steps.prompt: Match each model element to its meaning
pairs: Resistance seen looking into the input
Makes $v_o$ drop when load current flows
Internal resistance of the signal source
steps.explanation: $R_i$ and $R_o$ describe the amplifier's terminals, $A_{voc}$ its internal gain, and $R_s$ belongs to the source, not the amplifier. Together they let you predict the gain for any source and load.

steps.title: Loading effects
steps.body:
Not all of $v_s$ reaches the amplifier input and not all of $A_{voc}v_i$ reaches the load. Two voltage dividers are at work:
- input: $v_i = v_s\frac{R_i}{R_s+R_i}$
- output: $v_o = A_{voc}v_i\frac{R_L}{R_o+R_L}$
These reductions are called **loading effects**.

steps.prompt: Connecting a load $R_L$ to an amplifier with $R_o > 0$ makes the voltage gain $A_v = v_o/v_i$ smaller in magnitude than $A_{voc}$.
steps.explanation: True. Load current causes a drop across $R_o$, so $A_v = A_{voc}R_L/(R_o+R_L)$, which is less than $A_{voc}$ for any finite $R_L$. Only with $R_L \to \infty$ (open circuit) does $A_v$ equal $A_{voc}$.

steps.prompt: An amplifier has $A_{voc}$ = {{Avoc}} and $R_o$ = {{Ro|Ω}}. A load $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}} is connected. Find the loaded voltage gain $A_v = v_o/v_i$.
steps.explanation:
$R_o$ and $R_L$ form a voltage divider at the output:
$A_v = A_{voc}\frac{R_L}{R_o+R_L}$ = {{Avoc}} × {{RL|Ω}} / ({{Ro|Ω}} + {{RL|Ω}}) = {{Avoc*RL/(Ro+RL)}}.

steps.prompt: For an ideal voltage amplifier (no loading at input or output), the input and output resistances should be:
steps.explanation: With $R_i \to \infty$ the input divider $R_i/(R_s+R_i) \to 1$, so the full source voltage reaches the input. With $R_o \to 0$ the output divider $R_L/(R_o+R_L) \to 1$, so the output voltage does not depend on the load.

steps.prompt: An amplifier is driven by $v_i$ = {{vim*1000}} sin(2000π$t$) mV, which goes positive just after $t$ = 0. The graph shows the output $v_o$. Find the voltage gain $A_v$ (with its sign).
steps.explanation: The output peak is {{abs(A)*vim|V}} and the input peak {{vim|V}}, so $|A_v|$ = {{abs(A)*vim|V}} / {{vim|V}} = {{abs(A)}}. For the sign, compare the start: if the output first goes **down** while the input goes up, the amplifier is inverting and $A_v$ is negative. Here $A_v$ = {{A}}.

steps.prompt: A source $V_s$ = {{Vs|V}} rms with $R_s$ = {{Rs|Ω}} drives an amplifier with $R_i$ = {{Ri|Ω}}, $A_{voc}$ = {{Avoc}} and $R_o$ = {{Ro|Ω}}. The load is $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}. Find the rms output voltage $V_o$.
steps.explanation:
Input divider: $V_i = V_s\frac{R_i}{R_s+R_i}$ = {{Vs|V}} × {{Ri|Ω}}/({{Rs|Ω}} + {{Ri|Ω}}) = {{Vi|V}}.
Controlled source: $A_{voc}V_i$ = {{Avoc*Vi|V}}.
Output divider: $V_o = A_{voc}V_i\frac{R_L}{R_o+R_L}$ = {{Avoc*Vi|V}} × {{RL|Ω}}/({{Ro|Ω}} + {{RL|Ω}}) = {{Vo|V}}.

steps.prompt: An amplifier with input resistance $R_i$ = {{Ri|Ω}} drives a load $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}} with a loaded voltage gain $A_v$ = {{Av}}. Find the current gain $A_i = i_o/i_i$.
steps.explanation: $i_i = v_i/R_i$ and $i_o = v_o/R_L$, so $A_i = \frac{v_o/R_L}{v_i/R_i} = A_v\frac{R_i}{R_L}$ = {{Av}} × {{Ri|Ω}}/{{RL|Ω}} = {{Av*Ri/RL}}. A large $R_i$ keeps the input current tiny, so current gains are often huge.

steps.prompt: An amplifier has $A_v$ = {{Av}}, $R_i$ = {{Ri|Ω}} and drives a loudspeaker $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}. Find the power gain in decibels, $G_{dB}$.
steps.explanation:
$G = A_vA_i = A_v^2\frac{R_i}{R_L}$ = {{Av}}² × {{Ri|Ω}}/{{RL|Ω}} = {{Av^2*Ri/RL}}.
Power ratio → use $10\log_{10}$: $G_{dB} = 10\log_{10}$({{Av^2*Ri/RL}}) = {{10*log10(Av^2*Ri/RL)|dB}}.

steps.prompt: An amplifier has a voltage gain magnitude $|A_v|$ = {{Av}}. What is its voltage gain in decibels?
steps.explanation: For a voltage ratio use 20 log: $|A_v|_{dB} = 20\log_{10}$({{Av}}) = {{20*log10(Av)|dB}}. Using 10 log (the power-ratio rule) is the classic mistake; it gives {{10*log10(Av)|dB}}.

steps.prompt: Two amplifiers are cascaded. Stage 1: $A_{voc1}$ = {{A1}}, $R_{o1}$ = {{Ro1|Ω}}. Stage 2: $R_{i2}$ = {{Ri2|Ω}}, $A_{voc2}$ = {{A2}}, $R_{o2}$ = {{Ro2|Ω}}. Stage 2 drives $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}. Find the overall voltage gain $v_{o2}/v_{i1}$.
steps.explanation:
Stage 1 is loaded by $R_{i2}$: $A_{v1} = A_{voc1}\frac{R_{i2}}{R_{o1}+R_{i2}}$ = {{A1*Ri2/(Ri2+Ro1)}}.
Stage 2 is loaded by $R_L$: $A_{v2} = A_{voc2}\frac{R_L}{R_{o2}+R_L}$ = {{A2*RL/(RL+Ro2)}}.
Overall: $A_v = A_{v1}A_{v2}$ = {{A1*Ri2/(Ri2+Ro1)*A2*RL/(RL+Ro2)}}.

steps.prompt: An amplifier is powered by two supplies of {{V|V}} each (positive and negative rail). They deliver average currents $I_A$ = {{IA|A}} and $I_B$ = {{IB|A}}. The amplifier delivers $P_o$ = {{Po|W}} to the load. Find the efficiency $\eta$.

A single {{V|V}} supply delivers {{I|A}} to an amplifier, which delivers $P_o$ = {{Po|W}} to its load. The input signal power is negligible. How much power $P_d$ is dissipated as heat in the amplifier?
steps.explanation:
Power balance: $P_i + P_s = P_o + P_d$ with $P_i \approx 0$.
$P_s = VI$ = {{V}} × {{I}} = {{V*I|W}}, so $P_d = P_s - P_o$ = {{V*I|W}} − {{Po|W}} = {{V*I-Po|W}}.

steps.prompt: An amplifier delivers far more signal power to its load than it takes from the signal source. Where does the extra power come from?
steps.explanation: Power is conserved: $P_i + P_s = P_o + P_d$. The amplifier converts part of the dc supply power $P_s$ into signal power; the rest becomes heat $P_d$. The input only controls how that power is released.

steps.prompt: If two cascaded stages have voltage gains of 20 dB and 34 dB, the overall gain is 54 dB.
steps.explanation: True. Linear gains multiply ($A_v = A_{v1}A_{v2}$), and the log of a product is the sum of the logs, so dB gains add: 20 dB + 34 dB = 54 dB (a factor 10 × 50 = 500). The stage gains must already include loading.

steps.prompt: Tap the resistors that should be as **large** as possible so that $v_o$ comes close to $A_{voc}v_s$.
steps.explanation:
Two voltage dividers cause the loading:
$$v_o = A_{voc}v_s\cdot\frac{R_i}{R_s + R_i}\cdot\frac{R_L}{R_o + R_L}$$
Both fractions approach 1 when $R_i \gg R_s$ and $R_L \gg R_o$. So $R_i$ and $R_L$ should be large, while $R_s$ and $R_o$ should be small (an ideal voltage amplifier has $R_i = \infty$ and $R_o = 0$).

steps.prompt: An amplifier has $R_i$ = {{Ri|Ω}}, $A_{voc}$ = {{Avoc}}, $R_o$ = {{Ro|Ω}} and drives $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}. Find the power gain $G = P_o/P_i$ (as a ratio).
steps.explanation:
First the loaded voltage gain: $A_v = A_{voc}\frac{R_L}{R_o+R_L}$ = {{Av}}.
Then $A_i = A_v\frac{R_i}{R_L}$ = {{Av*Ri/RL}} and $G = A_vA_i = A_v^2\frac{R_i}{R_L}$ = {{Av^2*Ri/RL}} (= {{10*log10(Av^2*Ri/RL)|dB}}).

steps.prompt: Stage 1 ($A_{voc1}$ = {{A1}}, $R_{o1}$ = {{Ro1|Ω}}) drives stage 2 ($R_{i2}$ = {{Ri2|Ω}}, $A_{voc2}$ = {{A2}}). Find the open-circuit voltage gain $A_{voc}$ of the simplified model of the cascade.
steps.explanation:
Open-circuit gain means the **last** stage has no load, but stage 1 is still loaded by $R_{i2}$.
$A_{v1} = A_{voc1}\frac{R_{i2}}{R_{o1}+R_{i2}}$ = {{A1}} × {{Ri2|Ω}}/({{Ro1|Ω}} + {{Ri2|Ω}}) = {{A1*Ri2/(Ri2+Ro1)}}.
$A_{voc} = A_{v1}A_{voc2}$ = {{A1*Ri2/(Ri2+Ro1)}} × {{A2}} = {{A1*Ri2/(Ri2+Ro1)*A2}}.

steps.prompt: In the simplified model of a two-stage cascade, the input resistance $R_i$ and output resistance $R_o$ are:
steps.explanation: The source only sees the input of the first stage, so $R_i = R_{i1}$. The load only sees the output of the last stage, so $R_o = R_{o2}$. The inner resistances $R_{o1}$ and $R_{i2}$ only affect the overall gain $A_{voc}$.

steps.prompt: An amplifier produces $A_{voc}V_i$ = {{Avoc*Vi|V}} rms internally ($A_{voc}$ = {{Avoc}}, $V_i$ = {{Vi|V}}) and has $R_o$ = {{Ro|Ω}}. You may choose $R_L$ freely. What is the largest average power that can be delivered to the load?
steps.explanation: The output side is a Thévenin source $A_{voc}V_i$ with $R_t = R_o$, so maximum power transfer occurs for $R_L = R_o$ = {{Ro|Ω}}. Then $V_o = A_{voc}V_i/2$ = {{Avoc*Vi/2|V}} and $P_{o,max} = \frac{(A_{voc}V_i)^2}{4R_o}$ = {{Avoc*Vi|V}}²/(4 × {{Ro|Ω}}) = {{(Avoc*Vi)^2/(4*Ro)|W}}.

steps.prompt: A sensor ($V_s$ = {{Vs|V}}, $R_s$ = {{Rs|Ω}}) feeds an amplifier with $R_i$ = {{Ri|Ω}} and $R_o$ = {{Ro|Ω}} that drives $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}}. What open-circuit gain $A_{voc}$ is needed to get $V_o$ = {{Vo|V}}?
steps.explanation:
Write the overall gain with both dividers: $V_o = V_s\frac{R_i}{R_s+R_i}A_{voc}\frac{R_L}{R_o+R_L}$.
Input factor: {{Ri/(Rs+Ri)||4}}; output factor: {{RL/(Ro+RL)||4}}.
$A_{voc} = \frac{V_o/V_s}{(\text{input factor})(\text{output factor})}$ = {{Vo/Vs}}/({{Ri/(Rs+Ri)*RL/(Ro+RL)||4}}) = {{Vo/(Vs*Ri/(Rs+Ri)*RL/(Ro+RL))}}.

steps.prompt: A microphone preamp has a voltage gain of {{g1|dB}} and is followed by a stage with {{g2|dB}} (both include loading). What is the overall voltage gain magnitude as a plain ratio $|v_o/v_i|$?
An audio amplifier delivers $V_o$ = {{Vo|V}} rms to an $R_L$ = {{RL|Ω}} speaker. It runs from ±{{V|V}} supplies, each delivering an average current of {{I|A}}. Find the efficiency $\eta$.
steps.explanation:
Output power: $P_o = V_o^2/R_L$ = {{Vo}}²/{{RL}} = {{Vo^2/RL|W}}.
Supply power: $P_s = 2VI$ = 2 × {{V}} × {{I}} = {{2*V*I|W}}.
$\eta = P_o/P_s \times 100\%$ = {{(Vo^2/RL)/(2*V*I)*100|%}}. The rest, {{2*V*I-Vo^2/RL|W}}, heats the amplifier.
